description: Make a Max for Live device the producer asks for: a MIDI effect, an audio effect or an instrument. Kumi writes it to their User Library for load_device. Read the guide for the kind first (guide: true, type): how to patch it, where code belongs, the rules Kumi checks, and what makes a device good. To learn Max's objects (what each is for, its arguments, its inlets and outlets for the arguments given, its messages and attributes), give objects: ["pipe", "makenote 60 100 250"]: Kumi answers from this machine's Max, faster than the web and right for the Max the device runs in, and makes nothing. Then give its type, name, what it does, its controls (knobs, menus, switches and triggers, which become ordinary Live parameters, each in its group) and its patch: Max's own objects in Kumi's notation, with code only in the boxes that need it (GenExpr in [gen~], JavaScript in [v8] and [v8ui]). A device that's one box of code can be given as code instead: JavaScript for a MIDI effect, with tests Kumi runs; GenExpr for an audio effect, or for one voice of an instrument, which Kumi plays as many voices. Kumi builds the device around the patch or the code, lays its face out in Live's own style, keeps what plays in time on Live's grid with its building blocks ([kumi.clock], [kumi.notes], [kumi.transport]), gives a device that modulates a Map page of slots, checks it and always makes it: what's wrong comes back beside it, by line, with what Kumi changed to make it, and making it again in this conversation with the same name replaces it. Build what the producer asks for, as fully as they ask: as many controls as it needs, and the original's behaviour when recreating one. Kumi's rules keep a device safe and loadable; they don't limit its scope, and its ceilings are generous. Then load it with load_device and the itemId it returns, and hear an audio effect or instrument with audition. To change a device that's already there, Kumi's or anyone's, give from: alone, Kumi answers with the device in its notation, each box by name; with patch, controls or remove saying only what changes, it makes a new device from it and never writes the original's file.

guide.description: true: read how to make a device of this type (first)

objects.description: Max objects to learn, each as it's typed in a box ("makenote 60 100 250"): Kumi answers from this machine's Max and makes nothing

from.description: A device that's already there to start from: its file, its item in Live's Browser (user_library/…) or its name in the User Library

type.description: midi_effect, audio_effect or instrument; midi_effect when left out

name.description: The device's name, as the producer would say it

about.description: What it does, in a sentence or two

default.description: A number, one of the options, or true/false

group.description: The section of the face it's in, under this heading (controls that work together)

show.description: How it shows: a number as a dial (default), number box or slider; a choice as a menu (default) or tabs

patch.description: The device as a patch of Max's own objects in Kumi's notation, with code in [gen~], [v8] and [v8ui] boxes where objects do the job badly, and Kumi's building blocks for what plays in time (see the guide)

midi_effect:
Making a MIDI effect

Make it the way a Max user does: a patch of Max's own objects (patch), with code in a box only where objects do the job badly. A device that's one box of JavaScript can be given as code instead, with tests Kumi runs (the end of this guide).

Where code goes. Devices made by hand are mostly patches: Max's objects and messages do most of the work, and code is a small part. Put each job where it runs best:
- Timing: anything that plays in time with Live (steps, a sequencer, an arpeggiator, a clock, notes it times, an LFO or a gate in time with its bars) takes its time from Kumi's building blocks, [kumi.clock], [kumi.notes] and [kumi.transport] (Playing in time, below). They keep a device on Live's grid and tempo to the sample, through starts, stops, loops, jumps, tempo changes and a rate that moves. Max always runs JavaScript on its low-priority thread, where a message waits its turn: code can fill a table the clock's path reads, never sit between the clock and out.
- Whatever Max has an object for ([makenote], [pipe], [line~], [adsr~], [svf~], [tapin~]): the object, so the producer can see and change it.
- Sound made sample by sample with state or feedback (an oscillator, a filter, a delay that feeds back): [gen~] { GenExpr }.
- An algorithm with loops or tables (a Euclidean pattern, a scale, a random walk): [v8] { JavaScript }, off a path whose timing is crucial: it fills a table or answers a control, and the patch plays what it made.
- Drawing on the face: [v8ui] { JavaScript }.

Patching with Max's objects

Kumi reads each object's inlets and outlets from the installed Max, adds the face and lays the patch out top to bottom. It always makes the device: an object Max doesn't have, a port an object doesn't have, a message order left to where boxes sit, or a line it can't read comes back beside it, by line, with how to fix it, and making it again in this conversation with the same name replaces it.
- What an object takes and sends: make_device with objects (each as it's typed in a box) answers from this machine's Max with its arguments, its inlets and outlets for those arguments, its messages and its attributes. It's faster than the web and right for the Max the device runs in.
- A box per line: filter = [svf~ 1000 0.5] is an object, written as you'd type it in Max; (set $1) is a message box.
- Cords: a -> b -> c goes from outlet 0 to inlet 0; a.1 -> b.2 takes outlet 1 to inlet 2 (ports count from 0, left to right). A box written in a chain is a new box: "Cutoff" -> [sig~] -> filter.1.
- "Rate" is the control named Rate: it sends its value when it moves and when the device loads (a choice its option's index, a switch 0 or 1). Wire every control.
- in is the MIDI the device receives, as [midiin] sends it (bytes; [midiparse] takes them apart), and out takes MIDI on ([midiformat] puts it back together). Every note-on the device sends gets a note-off: [kumi.notes] ends its own notes, even when Live stops, and [midiflush] ends those held when a setting changes.
- [gen~] { … } holds GenExpr: in1, in2… are its inlets and out1, out2… its outlets, and a message "name value" sets its Param name (declare it: Param drive(1);).
- [v8 name] { … } holds JavaScript, embedded in the device (Max's v8): inlets = 2; and outlets = 2; at its top give it ports (one of each otherwise); a function named like a message answers it (bang(), msg_int(v), msg_float(v), list(), anything()); outlet(n, value) sends, and a number goes as outlet(n, "float", value), since Max can drop a bare outlet(n, 0). Code that doesn't parse is kept as written (Max says so in its console), and a cord to a port its code doesn't give is left out; both come back by line.
- [v8ui] { … } draws on the face in a section of its own, 160 by 150: mgraphics.init(); at its top, function paint() draws (mgraphics.set_source_rgba, rectangle, fill), and mgraphics.redraw() when a value arrives. Draw in the theme's colours: a dark display (0.09, 0.09, 0.09) with lines and text in Live's orange (1, 0.68, 0.34) reads in every theme.
- [p name] { … } holds a patch of its own: its [inlet]s and [outlet]s number from the left, in the order they're written.
- Order: Max sends an outlet's cords right to left by where their boxes sit. When one value feeds an object's cold inlet and its hot one, send it through [t] (trigger), whose outlets fire right to left: right outlet to the cold inlet, left to the hot one.
- Name sends, receives, buffers and dicts with --- (s ---lfo) so each copy of the device has its own. # starts a comment in the notation; a block's code keeps its own language's comments.

Playing in time

Kumi's building blocks are boxes in the patch that Kumi makes as subpatchers of Max's own objects, with their timing worked out and tested:
- clock = [kumi.clock 16n 8n 8nt]: steps on Live's grid, each on the sample it's due. Its arguments are the divisions its first inlet picks from by index (a Rate menu's: "Rate" -> clock; 1n, 2n, 4n, 8n, 16n and 32n when it has none, starting at 16n), and @length 16 and @swing 50 to start with. Inlets: the division (an index, or (beats 0.25)), swing (50 straight to 75) and the pattern's length in steps. Outlets: clock is each step's index (from 0) on the step; clock.1 is that step's length in ms at the tempo now, sent just before; clock.2 is 1 when Live starts and 0 when it stops. A division, swing or length that moves (by hand, automation or a mapping) lands on the next step of the new grid. It never doubles a step or puts one off the grid. After a start, a loop or a jump, the steps follow the song position: step 0 on the downbeat.
- Live takes a device's MIDI once per audio buffer, and a note due in a buffer's last signal vector goes out at the next buffer's start, up to a vector late (1.45 ms at 44.1 kHz). That's Max for Live's own limit, for every device; every other note goes out on its sample.
- notes = [kumi.notes]: plays notes and ends every one. Inlet 0 takes a pitch, or a list of pitch, velocity and length in ms; notes.1 a velocity; notes.2 a length in ms; notes -> out. Each note's end is in ms, so a stopped or jumped transport can't hold it up. Every held note ends when Live stops, when the device is turned off and when it's deleted, and a pitch played again before it ends is ended first. [kumi.notes 2] plays on channel 2.
- song = [kumi.transport]: Live's song position in beats at every sample (song, a signal), 1 while Live plays (song.1) and its tempo in BPM (song.2), for an LFO, gate or delay in time with Live's bars: song -> [gen~] { … }.
- A step sequencer, for instance, with controls "Rate", "Gate 1" … "Gate 16", "Note 1" … "Note 16": clock = [kumi.clock 16n 8n], "Rate" -> clock, clock -> step = [t i i i]; step.2 -> "Gate" -> open = [gate] (a step that's off lets no note through); step.1 -> playhead; step -> "Note" -> open.1; open -> notes = [kumi.notes]; clock.1 -> [* 0.5] -> notes.2 for a gate of half a step; notes -> out.
- Kumi checks what times notes, and says what's wrong with: steps made from plugsync~'s polled position, a clock that counts milliseconds or is off Live's grid (a [metro] without @quantize), and anything on Max's low-priority thread (code, [defer], [qmetro], the Live API) between a clock and out.

The face and the Map page

Kumi lays every face out the way Live's own devices look, in the producer's theme, dark or light. Don't style a device by editing its file after make_device; make it again with what should change.
- group: the section a control is in. Each group ("Clock", "Pattern", "Filter", "LFO") is a section with its name over it, in the order its first control is given, a line between sections.
- show: a number shows as a "dial" (its name and value; the default), a "number" box or a "slider"; a choice as a "menu" (the default) or "tabs". A switch is a button with its name, lit while on, and a trigger (type trigger) is one that's on only while it's pressed: Reset, Randomize, Tap.
- Controls named for a step ("Gate 1" … "Gate 16", "Note 1" … "Note 16", or "Step 1 Note") that the patch reads by step make a step grid, a row for each lane and a column for each step; each is an automatable parameter. In the patch, a lane's name reads it by step: clock -> "Note" sends the playing step's note (no cord from each step's control needed). Send the playing step's index (from 0) to playhead and it lights. Numbered controls the patch doesn't read by step ("Band 1 Freq" … "Band 4 Freq") stay ordinary controls.
- What a [v8ui] draws gets a section of its own.
- A device that modulates parameters (an LFO, an envelope, a step modulator, a follower) sends its modulation to mod, a signal from 0 to 1, and Kumi gives it a Map page of 8 slots (map: {"slots": 8}, at most 8), with tabs to switch between it and the main page. Each slot has a Map button that shows the parameter it maps once one's clicked, × to unmap, and Min and Max: the part of the modulation's range the source sweeps, in percent (Max below Min turns it upside down). It modulates the parameter from where its own control is, as Live's modulators do: one Live modulates both ways moves around its control, one it modulates one way from its minimum up to its control. It keeps its mapping with the Set and adds nothing to Live's undo. Several sources go to mod.0, mod.1… (named in map: {"sources": ["LFO 1", "LFO 2"]}), and each slot picks one. Don't make Map buttons of your own ([live.map], or code watching the selected parameter): Kumi's checks say so. A fixed target (this track's volume through [live.remote~]) is fine.

Code: a device that's one box of JavaScript

Your code runs inside Kumi's frame in Live's Max (JavaScript, v8, strict mode). You write functions and the frame calls them:
- function midi(event): required. Called for every MIDI message that arrives. What you don't send on is dropped, so pass(event) whatever the device doesn't change.
- function changed(name, value): optional. A control moved (a number; the option's text for a choice; true or false for a switch).
- function reset(): optional. Forget anything pending. Called on all-notes-off, after which the frame turns off every note the device still holds.

Events: { type, channel (1–16), time (ms) } and
- noteon, noteoff: pitch (0–127), velocity (0–127)
- cc: controller, value; pitchbend: value (0–16383, 8192 is the centre); aftertouch: value; polytouch: pitch, value; program: value

What your code can use:
- send(event) sends an event of that shape (channel defaults to 1, velocity to 100); pass(event) sends one on as it came.
- after(ms, fn) runs fn later and returns a timer; cancel(timer) stops it.
- params["Name"] is a control's value now; now() is the time in milliseconds.
- Plain JavaScript: Math, arrays, objects, Map, Set, classes. Not files, the network, or Max's and Live's objects: the frame hides them, and Kumi says so when code reaches for them.

What Kumi checks, saying beside the device what it found:
- Every note-on the device sends gets a note-off. When you delay, transpose or replace notes, send the note-off for the pitch you sent, not the one that arrived, and forget a pending note whose note-off comes first.
- Once every note is released, nothing is left running: cancel timers, or let them end. A device that runs free (an LFO, a clock, a generator that keeps sending on its own) gives runs_free: true instead: start its timer in the code and again in reset(), since an all-notes-off stops every timer.
- It runs without an error on a chord, a single note, a controller, a bend and aftertouch, and doesn't send without end.
- As many controls as the device needs (up to 128), each named in up to 32 characters (the producer's own words: letters, digits, spaces and . _ ( ) & ' + / # % -), with a range, a unit (ms, s, Hz, dB, %, st, note, pan, beats, bpm, x, or none) and a default that works on load. Past eight, the face shows them in up to three rows.

Craft:
- JavaScript in Max runs on its low-priority thread, so its timing can wander by a few milliseconds, and after() counts milliseconds, not Live's beats: right for grouping chords or delays of tens of milliseconds. A device that plays on its own in time with Live (a sequencer, an arpeggiator, a clock, a synced LFO) is a patch with [kumi.clock], not code.
- Keep midi() quick.
- For anything grouped in time (chords, strums), hold the note-ons for the window and close it early when a note-off arrives. The delay is the price of clean output; say so when it matters.
- Pass controllers, bend, aftertouch and program changes through unless changing them is the device's job.
- Choose sensible defaults and say what they are. Ask the producer at most one question, and only when a choice changes the result (such as delaying note-ons or retriggering); otherwise decide.

Tests: write 2 to 6 of what the device must do. Each has input events (with at, in ms), the events expected out in order (the fields you name are compared, and at to within 3 ms), and set for any control values. Kumi runs them and its own checks as it makes the device; a test that fails comes back beside it with what came out instead: fix the code or the test and call make_device again with the same name.

Then load_device with the itemId it returns, on the producer's MIDI track: Live puts a MIDI effect before the instrument. Tell the producer in a sentence or two what it does and what its controls are.

Kumi lays the face out (The face and the Map page, above). When a device loads, Kumi reads its face and says what a panel hides: you can't see Live, so say only what you know the producer will see.

- Operators you'll use: mix(a, b, t), clamp(x, lo, hi), tanh, abs, sqrt, pow, exp, sin, cos, dbtoa, atodb, mtof, ftom, mstosamps, phasor(hz), cycle(hz), triangle(phase, duty), noise(), slide(x, up, down), dcblock, latch, sah, change(x), delta, scale, fold, wrap, interp, and the constants samplerate, pi, twopi.

- Kumi's output stage follows your code: your output has NaN, denormals and DC taken out and is held under +6 dBFS (hard: a safety net against a runaway patch at the device's output, not a limiter to lean on); on an effect, Mix blends it with the dry signal, which passes untouched; Output sets the level. in1 and in2 are the left and right input; assign out1 and out2 (left, right) every sample. Kumi adds Mix (dry against your output) and Output knobs, so don't make your own.

Craft:
- Feedback: under 1 it dies away; at 1 or more it holds or self-oscillates, which some devices are made for (an infinite reverb, a delay that runs away, a resonator). Damp it (a one-pole lowpass in the loop), and at 1 or more put a saturator (tanh) in the loop too, so it settles at a level instead of growing without end.
- Smooth any control that changes delay times or gains quickly (slide, or a one-pole: y = mix(y, target, 0.001)), or it clicks.
- Reverbs: a few allpass diffusers into a feedback delay network, damped in the loop (Schroeder, Moorer, or a Dattorro plate). Delays: a Delay with feedback and a filter in the loop; ping-pong swaps channels. Saturation: tanh or a polynomial, with gain before and makeup after. Filters: one-poles and biquads from History.
- Choose sensible defaults, so it sounds right when it loads.

Max compiles the code when Live loads the device. If it doesn't compile, the device lets no sound through: after loading it (load_device with the itemId, onto the track), hear it with audition, playing audio through that track, and against the reference if the producer gave one. A silent render means fix the code.

Kumi lays the face out (The face and the Map page, above). When a device loads, Kumi reads its face and says what a panel hides: you can't see Live, so say only what you know the producer will see.
instrument:
Making an instrument

Make it the way a Max user does: a patch of Max's own objects (patch), with code in a box only where objects do the job badly. An instrument that's one voice of GenExpr can be given as code instead, and Kumi plays it as many voices (the end of this guide).

Where code goes. Devices made by hand are mostly patches: Max's objects and messages do most of the work, and code is a small part. Put each job where it runs best:
- Timing: anything that plays in time with Live (steps, a sequencer, an arpeggiator, a clock, notes it times, an LFO or a gate in time with its bars) takes its time from Kumi's building blocks, [kumi.clock], [kumi.notes] and [kumi.transport] (Playing in time, below). They keep a device on Live's grid and tempo to the sample, through starts, stops, loops, jumps, tempo changes and a rate that moves. Max always runs JavaScript on its low-priority thread, where a message waits its turn: code can fill a table the clock's path reads, never sit between the clock and out.
- Whatever Max has an object for ([makenote], [pipe], [line~], [adsr~], [svf~], [tapin~]): the object, so the producer can see and change it.
- Sound made sample by sample with state or feedback (an oscillator, a filter, a delay that feeds back): [gen~] { GenExpr }.
- An algorithm with loops or tables (a Euclidean pattern, a scale, a random walk): [v8] { JavaScript }, off a path whose timing is crucial: it fills a table or answers a control, and the patch plays what it made.
- Drawing on the face: [v8ui] { JavaScript }.

Patching with Max's objects

Kumi reads each object's inlets and outlets from the installed Max, adds the face and lays the patch out top to bottom. It always makes the device: an object Max doesn't have, a port an object doesn't have, a message order left to where boxes sit, or a line it can't read comes back beside it, by line, with how to fix it, and making it again in this conversation with the same name replaces it.
- What an object takes and sends: make_device with objects (each as it's typed in a box) answers from this machine's Max with its arguments, its inlets and outlets for those arguments, its messages and its attributes. It's faster than the web and right for the Max the device runs in.
- A box per line: filter = [svf~ 1000 0.5] is an object, written as you'd type it in Max; (set $1) is a message box.
- Cords: a -> b -> c goes from outlet 0 to inlet 0; a.1 -> b.2 takes outlet 1 to inlet 2 (ports count from 0, left to right). A box written in a chain is a new box: "Cutoff" -> [sig~] -> filter.1.
- "Rate" is the control named Rate: it sends its value when it moves and when the device loads (a choice its option's index, a switch 0 or 1). Wire every control.
- in is the track's MIDI, as [midiin] sends it (bytes; [midiparse]'s first outlet is pitch and velocity); send the sound's left and right to out.0 and out.1. Kumi's output stage follows (Output). voices is for code: a patch plays the notes it's patched to.
- [gen~] { … } holds GenExpr: in1, in2… are its inlets and out1, out2… its outlets, and a message "name value" sets its Param name (declare it: Param drive(1);).
- [v8 name] { … } holds JavaScript, embedded in the device (Max's v8): inlets = 2; and outlets = 2; at its top give it ports (one of each otherwise); a function named like a message answers it (bang(), msg_int(v), msg_float(v), list(), anything()); outlet(n, value) sends, and a number goes as outlet(n, "float", value), since Max can drop a bare outlet(n, 0). Code that doesn't parse is kept as written (Max says so in its console), and a cord to a port its code doesn't give is left out; both come back by line.
- [v8ui] { … } draws on the face in a section of its own, 160 by 150: mgraphics.init(); at its top, function paint() draws (mgraphics.set_source_rgba, rectangle, fill), and mgraphics.redraw() when a value arrives. Draw in the theme's colours: a dark display (0.09, 0.09, 0.09) with lines and text in Live's orange (1, 0.68, 0.34) reads in every theme.
- [p name] { … } holds a patch of its own: its [inlet]s and [outlet]s number from the left, in the order they're written.
- Order: Max sends an outlet's cords right to left by where their boxes sit. When one value feeds an object's cold inlet and its hot one, send it through [t] (trigger), whose outlets fire right to left: right outlet to the cold inlet, left to the hot one.
- Name sends, receives, buffers and dicts with --- (s ---lfo) so each copy of the device has its own. # starts a comment in the notation; a block's code keeps its own language's comments.

GenExpr is the language of Max's gen~: C-like, run once per sample. Variables need no declaring; every statement ends with a semicolon.
- Its order is fixed: your function definitions first (name(a, b) { ... return x; }), then declarations (History, Delay, Data), then statements. Kumi puts the Params for your controls after your functions.
- Each control is a Param, named like it: a control "Decay Time" is decay_time in the code (Kumi declares it: read it, and don't declare it again). A number control is its value; a choice is its option's index (0, 1, …); a switch is 0 or 1. Don't name functions or variables like a control's Param.
- History x(0); keeps x from one sample to the next (filters, envelopes, feedback). Delay d(samplerate); is a delay line up to one second long (d.write(v); y = d.read(mstosamps(ms)); interp="linear" in the declaration or the read makes it smooth). Data t(512); is a table (peek, poke).
- Operators you'll use: mix(a, b, t), clamp(x, lo, hi), tanh, abs, sqrt, pow, exp, sin, cos, dbtoa, atodb, mtof, ftom, mstosamps, phasor(hz), cycle(hz), triangle(phase, duty), noise(), slide(x, up, down), dcblock, latch, sah, change(x), delta, scale, fold, wrap, interp, and the constants samplerate, pi, twopi.
- Use samplerate, never 44100: Live runs at whatever rate the producer set.
- Kumi's output stage follows your code: your output has NaN, denormals and DC taken out and is held under +6 dBFS (hard: a safety net against a runaway patch at the device's output, not a limiter to lean on); on an effect, Mix blends it with the dry signal, which passes untouched; Output sets the level. Inside your code nothing is capped: feedback, gain and self-oscillation are yours.
- Give the device as many controls as it needs (up to 128): when recreating a device, all of the original's. Past eight, the face shows them in up to three rows.

Playing in time

Kumi's building blocks are boxes in the patch that Kumi makes as subpatchers of Max's own objects, with their timing worked out and tested:
- clock = [kumi.clock 16n 8n 8nt]: steps on Live's grid, each on the sample it's due. Its arguments are the divisions its first inlet picks from by index (a Rate menu's: "Rate" -> clock; 1n, 2n, 4n, 8n, 16n and 32n when it has none, starting at 16n), and @length 16 and @swing 50 to start with. Inlets: the division (an index, or (beats 0.25)), swing (50 straight to 75) and the pattern's length in steps. Outlets: clock is each step's index (from 0) on the step; clock.1 is that step's length in ms at the tempo now, sent just before; clock.2 is 1 when Live starts and 0 when it stops. A division, swing or length that moves (by hand, automation or a mapping) lands on the next step of the new grid. It never doubles a step or puts one off the grid. After a start, a loop or a jump, the steps follow the song position: step 0 on the downbeat.
- Live takes a device's MIDI once per audio buffer, and a note due in a buffer's last signal vector goes out at the next buffer's start, up to a vector late (1.45 ms at 44.1 kHz). That's Max for Live's own limit, for every device; every other note goes out on its sample.
- notes = [kumi.notes]: plays notes and ends every one. Inlet 0 takes a pitch, or a list of pitch, velocity and length in ms; notes.1 a velocity; notes.2 a length in ms; notes -> out. Each note's end is in ms, so a stopped or jumped transport can't hold it up. Every held note ends when Live stops, when the device is turned off and when it's deleted, and a pitch played again before it ends is ended first. [kumi.notes 2] plays on channel 2.
- song = [kumi.transport]: Live's song position in beats at every sample (song, a signal), 1 while Live plays (song.1) and its tempo in BPM (song.2), for an LFO, gate or delay in time with Live's bars: song -> [gen~] { … }.
- A step sequencer, for instance, with controls "Rate", "Gate 1" … "Gate 16", "Note 1" … "Note 16": clock = [kumi.clock 16n 8n], "Rate" -> clock, clock -> step = [t i i i]; step.2 -> "Gate" -> open = [gate] (a step that's off lets no note through); step.1 -> playhead; step -> "Note" -> open.1; open -> notes = [kumi.notes]; clock.1 -> [* 0.5] -> notes.2 for a gate of half a step; notes -> out.
- Kumi checks what times notes, and says what's wrong with: steps made from plugsync~'s polled position, a clock that counts milliseconds or is off Live's grid (a [metro] without @quantize), and anything on Max's low-priority thread (code, [defer], [qmetro], the Live API) between a clock and out.

The face and the Map page

Kumi lays every face out the way Live's own devices look, in the producer's theme, dark or light. Don't style a device by editing its file after make_device; make it again with what should change.
- group: the section a control is in. Each group ("Clock", "Pattern", "Filter", "LFO") is a section with its name over it, in the order its first control is given, a line between sections.
- show: a number shows as a "dial" (its name and value; the default), a "number" box or a "slider"; a choice as a "menu" (the default) or "tabs". A switch is a button with its name, lit while on, and a trigger (type trigger) is one that's on only while it's pressed: Reset, Randomize, Tap.
- Controls named for a step ("Gate 1" … "Gate 16", "Note 1" … "Note 16", or "Step 1 Note") that the patch reads by step make a step grid, a row for each lane and a column for each step; each is an automatable parameter. In the patch, a lane's name reads it by step: clock -> "Note" sends the playing step's note (no cord from each step's control needed). Send the playing step's index (from 0) to playhead and it lights. Numbered controls the patch doesn't read by step ("Band 1 Freq" … "Band 4 Freq") stay ordinary controls.
- What a [v8ui] draws gets a section of its own.
- A device that modulates parameters (an LFO, an envelope, a step modulator, a follower) sends its modulation to mod, a signal from 0 to 1, and Kumi gives it a Map page of 8 slots (map: {"slots": 8}, at most 8), with tabs to switch between it and the main page. Each slot has a Map button that shows the parameter it maps once one's clicked, × to unmap, and Min and Max: the part of the modulation's range the source sweeps, in percent (Max below Min turns it upside down). It modulates the parameter from where its own control is, as Live's modulators do: one Live modulates both ways moves around its control, one it modulates one way from its minimum up to its control. It keeps its mapping with the Set and adds nothing to Live's undo. Several sources go to mod.0, mod.1… (named in map: {"sources": ["LFO 1", "LFO 2"]}), and each slot picks one. Don't make Map buttons of your own ([live.map], or code watching the selected parameter): Kumi's checks say so. A fixed target (this track's volume through [live.remote~]) is fine.

Code: one voice of GenExpr, played as many voices

You write one voice, and Kumi plays copies of it (voices: 8 when left out, up to 32, 1 for a mono synth), sharing out the notes and taking the oldest voice when all are busy. Each voice gets, besides your controls:
- note: the MIDI note it plays (mtof(note + bend) is its frequency)
- velocity: 0–127, and 0 once the key is released (start the release then)
- strike: a new number for every note played: change(strike) != 0 is the moment a note starts, even when a busy voice is taken for one at the same velocity (start the attack then)
- bend: pitch bend in semitones (±2); mod_wheel: 0–1
Assign out1 and out2 (left, right). There's no audio input. Kumi adds an Output knob.

Craft:
- Envelopes from History: on a strike, restart the attack; while velocity > 0, rise to the sustain; once it's 0, fall (exp(-1 / (seconds * samplerate)) per sample makes an exponential decay).
- Voices add up: keep one voice around 0.2 at full velocity, so a chord stays well under 0 dBFS.
- Oscillators: phasor(freq) is a rising ramp 0–1 (a saw once scaled to -1..1; it aliases, so filter it or use a polyBLEP), cycle(freq) a sine, triangle(phasor(freq), 0.5) a triangle, noise() white noise. Detune by adding cents: mtof(note + bend + cents / 100).
- A filter with its cutoff following an envelope does most of the work in subtractive sounds; FM is cycle(freq + cycle(freq * ratio) * index * freq).
- Choose sensible defaults, so it plays well when it loads.

Max compiles the code when Live loads the device. If it doesn't compile, the instrument is silent: after loading it (load_device with the itemId onto a MIDI track), write a short clip and hear it with audition. A silent render means fix the code.

Kumi lays the face out (The face and the Map page, above). When a device loads, Kumi reads its face and says what a panel hides: you can't see Live, so say only what you know the producer will see.
